subject: English
description: Direct ↔ indirect speech — tense-shift rules, modal/pronoun changes, time/place expressions, statements/questions/commands.

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech: 'He said, "I am happy."'

options.option_text: He said that he was happy
He said that I am happy here
He says that he is happy now
He told that I was happy here

questions.explanation: DIRECT → INDIRECT (REPORTED) speech RULES: (1) PRONOUNS shift to maintain reporter's perspective: 'I' → 'he/she' (depending on speaker's gender). (2) TENSE shifts BACK if reporting verb is in PAST tense: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; past simple → past perfect. (3) Add 'THAT' (often optional in indirect statements). (4) Remove QUOTES. EXAMPLE: 'He said, "I am happy"' → 'He said THAT he WAS happy.' KEY TENSE SHIFT TABLE: (a) am/is/are → was/were. (b) do/does → did. (c) was/were → had been. (d) have/has → had. (e) had → had. (f) will → would. (g) shall → should/would. (h) can → could. (i) may → might. (j) must → had to (or unchanged). EXCEPTIONS to tense shift (when truth is universal/eternal): (1) Universal facts: 'He said that the sun rises in the east' (no shift, 'rises' — universal truth). (2) Habitual actions in present: sometimes preserved. WHEN reporting verb is PRESENT: 'He says, "I am happy"' → 'He says (that) he is happy' (no tense shift). PRACTICE: 'They said, "We will come"' → 'They said they WOULD come.' (NOT 'will'). PYQ FREQUENCY: direct/indirect basic conversion in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre 1-2× per cycle.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert: 'She said, "I will go to the market tomorrow."'

options.option_text: She said that she would go to the market the next day
She said that she will go tomorrow market here
She said she is going to market today (not this)
She said that I would go market tomorrow (not this)

questions.explanation: TWO CHANGES: (1) WILL → WOULD (modal shift in indirect). (2) TOMORROW → THE NEXT DAY (time-expression shift). KEY TIME/PLACE EXPRESSIONS that change in REPORTED SPEECH: (a) NOW → THEN. (b) TODAY → THAT DAY. (c) TOMORROW → THE NEXT DAY / THE FOLLOWING DAY. (d) YESTERDAY → THE PREVIOUS DAY / THE DAY BEFORE. (e) THIS → THAT. (f) THESE → THOSE. (g) HERE → THERE. (h) AGO → BEFORE. (i) LAST week/month → THE PREVIOUS week/month. (j) NEXT week/month → THE FOLLOWING week/month. SAMPLE: 'He said, "I bought it yesterday"' → 'He said he had bought it the day before.' ANOTHER: 'She said, "I am here now"' → 'She said she was there then.' KEY TENSE SHIFT for MODALS: (1) will → would. (2) shall → should. (3) can → could. (4) may → might. (5) must → had to (or unchanged for general moral obligation). PRACTICE: 'He said, "I can swim"' → 'He said he could swim.' 'She said, "You must come"' → 'She said I had to come / he must come' (depends). FUTURE-IN-PAST: 'would' is the past form of 'will' — used when REPORTING a future-tense statement IN THE PAST. PYQ FREQUENCY: time-expression shifts in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI English 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert: 'She asked, "Where do you live?"'

options.option_text: She asked where I lived
She asked where do I live there
She asked that I lived where then
She told me where I lived right then

questions.explanation: REPORTED QUESTION rules: (1) Use 'asked', 'inquired' (NOT 'said'). (2) For WH-QUESTIONS (who, what, where, when, why, how): keep WH-WORD + change tense + reorder to STATEMENT structure (no auxiliary inversion). 'Where do you live?' → 'where I lived' (WH + subject + verb; do dropped, tense shifted). (3) For YES/NO QUESTIONS (no WH-word): use 'IF' or 'WHETHER'. 'Are you coming?' → 'asked if I was coming.' KEY: NO QUESTION MARK in indirect; statement form. NO AUXILIARY 'do/does/did' (it's absorbed into tense shift). EXAMPLES: (1) 'He asked, "What is your name?"' → 'He asked what my name was.' (2) 'She asked, "Will you help?"' → 'She asked if I would help.' (3) 'They asked, "Where are we going?"' → 'They asked where they were going.' (4) 'I said, "Have you eaten?"' → 'I asked if she/he had eaten.' KEY TRAPS: (a) Don't keep 'do/does/did' in indirect: WRONG: 'asked where do I live'. (b) Don't add 'that': WRONG: 'asked that where I lived'. (c) Don't keep '?': WRONG: 'asked where I lived?' INDIRECT QUESTIONS take period (.), not question mark. PYQ FREQUENCY: WH-question conversion in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert imperatives: 'The teacher said, "Open your books."'

options.option_text: The teacher told us to open our books
The teacher said that we open the books
The teacher told that we should open books
The teacher asked open the books

questions.explanation: IMPERATIVE → INDIRECT speech: use 'TOLD/ORDERED/COMMANDED + object + TO + base verb'. 'Open your books' → 'told us to OPEN our books'. KEY: (1) Use 'TO + base verb' (infinitive). (2) PRONOUNS shift (your → our). (3) Choose appropriate REPORTING VERB based on tone: (a) NEUTRAL: 'told' (most common). (b) AUTHORITATIVE: 'ordered', 'commanded', 'demanded'. (c) ADVISORY: 'advised', 'suggested', 'recommended'. (d) REQUEST: 'requested', 'asked'. (e) PROHIBITIVE: 'forbade', 'told NOT TO'. (f) WARNING: 'warned'. PRACTICE: (1) 'Stop!' → 'told me to stop' / 'commanded me to stop'. (2) 'Please come early' → 'requested me to come early.' (3) 'Don't be late' → 'told me not to be late' / 'warned me against being late.' (4) 'Help your sister' → 'asked me to help my sister.' (5) 'Always speak the truth' → 'advised me to always speak the truth.' NEGATIVE IMPERATIVES: 'Don't smoke' → 'told me NOT TO smoke' OR 'forbade me to smoke.' KEY: TO + V1 structure for imperatives. SUGGESTIONS: 'Let's go' → 'suggested going' or 'proposed that we should go.' EXAM TRAP: students mistakenly say 'told me that I should open' — INCORRECT for imperative; should use TO + V1. PYQ FREQUENCY: imperative conversion in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert exclamations: 'He said, "What a beautiful sunset!"'

options.option_text: He exclaimed that the sunset was beautiful
He said what a beautiful sunset there
He exclaimed the sunset is very beautiful
He told that the beautiful sunset was here

questions.explanation: EXCLAMATIONS → INDIRECT speech: use 'EXCLAIMED' (or 'cried out', 'shouted') + 'that' + adjective transformed into normal form. PATTERN: 'What a/an + ADJ + N!' → 'exclaimed that the/a + N + was/were + ADJ.' EXAMPLE: 'What a beautiful sunset!' → 'exclaimed that the sunset was beautiful.' KEY TRANSFORMATION: (1) REPORTING VERB: 'said' → 'exclaimed' (or 'said with joy/sorrow/surprise', etc.). (2) DROP exclamation words: WHAT, HOW, ALAS, OH, WOW. (3) USE 'THAT' to introduce. (4) RESTRUCTURE: '(adj) + (noun)' → '(noun) + was/were + (adj)'. PRACTICE: (1) 'Hurrah! We won!' → 'shouted joyfully that they had won.' (2) 'Alas! He is dead.' → 'lamented that he was dead.' (3) 'How tall the building is!' → 'exclaimed that the building was very tall.' (4) 'Oh! It's raining' → 'exclaimed that it was raining.' KEY EMOTIONAL VERBS for exclamation: (a) JOY: rejoiced, shouted with joy, exclaimed joyfully. (b) SORROW: lamented, mourned, regretted. (c) SURPRISE: exclaimed with surprise, cried out. (d) FEAR: cried out in fear, screamed. (e) PRAISE: applauded, praised. EXAM-FAVOURITE: pick reporting verb that captures EMOTIONAL TONE of original exclamation. PYQ FREQUENCY: exclamation conversion in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert: 'He said, "The earth revolves around the sun."'

options.option_text: He said that the earth revolves around the sun
He said that the earth revolved around the sun
He told the earth had revolved sun (not this)
He said earth was revolving around sun

questions.explanation: EXCEPTION to TENSE-SHIFT RULE: When the reported speech expresses a UNIVERSAL TRUTH, SCIENTIFIC FACT, or HABITUAL ACTION (eternally true), TENSE DOES NOT SHIFT. 'The earth revolves around the sun' is a permanent astronomical fact — KEEP 'revolves' in present tense. KEY EXCEPTIONS to tense shift: (1) UNIVERSAL TRUTHS: 'Sun rises in the east' — present continues. (2) SCIENTIFIC FACTS: 'Water boils at 100°C' — present. (3) PROVERBS: 'Honesty is the best policy' — present. (4) HISTORICAL FACTS (sometimes; debated): 'India became independent in 1947' — usually past simple OK either way. (5) MATHEMATICAL FACTS: 'Two plus two equals four' — present. (6) HABITUAL ACTIONS in present (sometimes): 'I exercise daily.' SAMPLE — exam variations: (a) 'He said, "Honesty is the best policy"' → 'He said that honesty IS the best policy' (NOT 'was'). (b) 'She said, "Boiling point of water is 100°C"' → present preserved. (c) 'Galileo said, "The earth moves"' → present preserved (universal). EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: students mechanically apply tense shift, missing the universal-truth exception. WHEN UNCERTAIN: if the statement holds eternally, KEEP present; if it's a momentary observation, SHIFT to past. PYQ FREQUENCY: universal-truth exception in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert: 'They said, "We bought a car last month."'

options.option_text: They said that they had bought a car the previous month
They said that we bought a car last month here
They said they bought car some month ago there
They told that we will buy a car next month here

questions.explanation: TWO MAIN CHANGES: (1) PAST SIMPLE 'bought' → PAST PERFECT 'had bought' (tense shift). (2) 'LAST MONTH' → 'THE PREVIOUS MONTH' (time-expression shift). PRONOUN: 'we' (refers to 'they' the speakers in this case) → 'they'. KEY TENSE SHIFTS for past tenses: (1) PAST SIMPLE → PAST PERFECT: 'I went' → 'he had gone'. (2) PAST CONTINUOUS → PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS: 'I was eating' → 'he had been eating'. (3) PAST PERFECT → PAST PERFECT (no further shift, already perfect): 'I had finished' → 'he had finished'. (4) PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS → no further shift. PRESENT TENSE SHIFTS: (1) PRESENT SIMPLE → PAST SIMPLE: 'I work' → 'he worked'. (2) PRESENT CONTINUOUS → PAST CONTINUOUS: 'I am working' → 'he was working'. (3) PRESENT PERFECT → PAST PERFECT: 'I have worked' → 'he had worked'. SAMPLE: 'I have lived here for 10 years' → 'he had lived there for 10 years.' KEY EXCEPTIONS: when the situation is STILL TRUE / RECENTLY TRUE: '(a) She said, "I am pregnant"' → if she's still pregnant, may keep 'I am' — but most exams shift to 'was'. (b) Universal truths — no shift. PYQ FREQUENCY: complex multi-shift problems in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains, RBI English 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic application of multiple rules.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct indirect speech of: 'He said to her, "Have you finished the report?"'

options.option_text: He asked her that she has finished the report
He asked her whether she had finished the report
He asked her whether she finished the report
He told her if she had finished the report

questions.explanation: B is correct: yes/no questions in indirect speech use 'if' or 'whether' as the connector, and the present perfect 'have finished' backshifts to past perfect 'had finished'. A is wrong because 'that' is the connector for statements, not questions. C correctly uses 'whether' but fails to backshift the tense. D uses 'told' which is ungrammatical without a direct reporting-verb object before a question clause.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts the following into indirect speech: 'The doctor said to him, "Take rest for a week."'

options.option_text: The doctor told him that he takes rest for a week
The doctor advised him to take rest for a week
The doctor suggested him to take rest for a week
The doctor requested him that he took rest for a week

questions.explanation: B is correct: imperatives given for someone's benefit are reported using 'advise + object + infinitive'. C is the most tempting distractor, but 'suggest' cannot take 'object + infinitive' in standard grammar — it requires 'suggest + gerund' or 'suggest + that-clause'. A wrongly treats the imperative as a statement. D uses 'that' with 'requested', which should be 'requested + object + to + infinitive'.

questions.stem: 'She said, "I may not be able to attend the meeting."' — Which of the following is the correct reported form?

options.option_text: She said that she might not be able to attend the meeting
She said that she may not be able to attend the meeting
She said that she could not be able to attend the meeting
She said that she should not be able to attend the meeting

questions.explanation: A is correct: the modal 'may' backshifts to 'might' when the reporting verb is in the past tense. B is the most common error — retaining 'may' unchanged. C wrongly substitutes 'could', which conveys ability rather than possibility. D uses 'should', which carries a sense of obligation/advice, completely altering the original meaning.

questions.stem: 'He said to me, "I will call you here tomorrow."' — Identify the fully correct indirect speech.

options.option_text: He told me that he would call me there the next day
He told me that he would call me here the next day
He said to me that he will call me there tomorrow
He told me that I would call him there the following day

questions.explanation: A is correct: three simultaneous shifts are required — 'will → would' (modal backshift), 'here → there' (place adverb shift), and 'tomorrow → the next day' (time adverb shift). B correctly shifts tense and time but fails to change 'here → there'. C retains 'will' and 'tomorrow' unchanged. D wrongly shifts the pronoun 'you' (the addressee) to 'I', inverting who makes the call.

questions.stem: 'She said, "I started learning French two years ago."' — Which reported form handles ALL shifts correctly?

options.option_text: She said that she had started learning French two years ago
She said that she started learning French two years before
She said that she has started learning French two years before
She said that she had started learning French two years before

questions.explanation: D is correct: simple past 'started' must backshift to past perfect 'had started', and the time adverb 'ago' must change to 'before' in indirect speech. A correctly backshifts the tense but retains 'ago' — a very frequent exam error. B changes 'ago → before' but leaves the tense unshifted. C uses present perfect 'has started', which is doubly wrong (wrong tense shift and 'before' is correct but redundant with a non-backshifted form).

questions.stem: 'He said, "Let us not waste time on unnecessary arguments."' — Which reported form is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: He suggested them not to waste time on unnecessary arguments
He proposed that they should not waste time on unnecessary arguments
He told that they should not waste time on unnecessary arguments
He suggested that they would not waste time on unnecessary arguments

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Let us…' expressing a collective suggestion is reported as 'proposed/suggested that + subject + should + base verb'. A is the classic trap — 'suggest' cannot be followed by 'object + to-infinitive' ('suggested them not to' is ungrammatical). C uses 'told' without a required direct object, making it ungrammatical. D uses 'would', which implies volition or prediction rather than suggestion.

questions.stem: 'She said, "If I had known about the vacancy, I would have applied."' — Which reported form is correct?

options.option_text: She said that if she has known about the vacancy, she would apply
She said that if she knew about the vacancy, she would have applied
She said that if she had known about the vacancy, she would have applied
She told that if she had known about the vacancy, she would had applied

questions.explanation: C is correct: third conditionals (past perfect + would have) do NOT backshift in reported speech — they are already at the grammatical limit of the past. A wrongly shifts to present perfect and drops the perfect aspect in the result clause. B changes the condition to simple past, converting a third conditional to a second conditional — a serious structural error. D incorrectly uses 'would had applied' (should be 'would have applied') and 'told' without a direct object.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct indirect form of: 'She asked me, "Have you finished your homework?"'?

options.option_text: She asked me if I had finished my homework.
She asked me that had I finished my homework.
She asked me whether I have finished my homework.
She asked me that I had finished my homework.

questions.explanation: Yes/No questions use 'if' or 'whether' (never 'that') and follow statement word order with tense backshift: 'have finished' → 'had finished'. Option C is the prime trap — it correctly uses 'whether' but fails to backshift, retaining the present perfect 'have finished' instead of shifting to 'had finished'. Options B and D both wrongly use 'that', which is reserved for statement reporting, not question reporting.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts to indirect speech: 'Ravi said to Meena, "I have lost your book."'?

options.option_text: Ravi told Meena that I had lost your book right then.
Ravi told Meena that he had lost her book.
Ravi told Meena that he has lost her book just then.
Ravi said Meena that he had lost her book afterward.

questions.explanation: 'Said to' becomes 'told'; first-person 'I' shifts to 'he' (Ravi), second-person 'your' shifts to 'her' (Meena's book), and present perfect 'have lost' backshifts to past perfect 'had lost'. Option C correctly shifts the pronoun but retains 'has lost' without backshifting. Option A fails on pronouns — 'I' and 'your' are unchanged. Option D uses 'said Meena', which is ungrammatical: 'said' cannot take a person as indirect object without 'to'.

questions.stem: Select the correct indirect speech for: 'The officer said, "The results may be declared tomorrow."'

options.option_text: The officer said that the results may be declared the next day.
The officer said that the results might be declared the next day.
The officer said that the results would be declared the next day.
The officer said that the results might have declared the next day.

questions.explanation: Modal 'may' backshifts to 'might', and time adverb 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'. Option A is the most tempting wrong answer — it changes the time expression correctly but forgets to backshift 'may' to 'might'. Option C uses 'would', converting a possibility into a near-certainty or intention, which distorts meaning. Option D produces an incorrect active construction 'might have declared'; the passive 'might have been declared' would at least be structurally valid, but 'might be declared' is the correct backshift here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct indirect speech for: 'Rohit said, "Let us form a study group."'?

options.option_text: Rohit said that let them form a study group there.
Rohit told that they should form a study group then.
Rohit suggested that they should form a study group.
Rohit proposed them to form a study group at once.

questions.explanation: 'Let us' signals a proposal; the standard reporting verb is 'suggested' followed by 'that + subject + should + base verb'. Option A wrongly drags the imperative 'let' into the indirect clause — a common structural error. Option B uses 'told that' without the mandatory indirect object ('told them that'). Option D misuses 'proposed them to': 'propose' requires a 'that-clause', not a person + infinitive structure.

questions.stem: Identify the correctly converted indirect speech for: 'She told her sister, "You have been wasting your time lately."'

options.option_text: She told to her sister that she had been wasting her time lately.
She told her sister that you have been wasting your time lately.
She told her sister that she has been wasting her time these days.
She told her sister that she had been wasting her time lately.

questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous 'have been wasting' → past perfect continuous 'had been wasting'; 'you' → 'she'; 'your' → 'her'; 'lately' stays unchanged as it is already a relative time expression. Option A inserts an incorrect 'to' after 'told' — 'told' is a ditransitive verb that never takes 'to' before its indirect object. Option B keeps 'you' and 'your' without pronoun shift. Option C fails to backshift ('has been' instead of 'had been') and also wrongly replaces 'lately' with 'these days', which alters meaning.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly converts to indirect speech: 'The accused said, "I did not forge the documents."'?

options.option_text: The accused denied having forged the documents.
The accused denied to forge any of the documents then.
The accused denied that he had not forged the documents.
The accused refused having forged the documents then.

questions.explanation: A negative first-person statement is idiomatically reported using 'denied + gerund' (or 'denied having + past participle'). Option B uses 'denied to forge' — 'deny' never takes a to-infinitive, making this ungrammatical. Option C is the craftiest distractor: 'denied that he had NOT forged' creates a logical double negative, semantically implying he affirmed the forgery. Option D uses 'refused', which denotes unwillingness to do a future action, not rejection of a past act.

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts to indirect speech: 'My father said, "Unless you repay the loan, the bank will seize your property."'?

options.option_text: My father said that until I repaid the loan, the bank would seize my property.
My father told me that unless I repaid the loan, the bank would seize my property.
My father said that unless I will repay the loan, the bank would seize my property.
My father said me that unless I repaid the loan, the bank will seize my property.

questions.explanation: Three simultaneous changes are required: (1) 'said' → 'told me' (reporting verb must take an indirect object when addressed to a person); (2) 'you'→'I' and 'your'→'my' (pronoun shift to the speaker's perspective, since the father was addressing the reporter); (3) backshift 'repay'→'repaid' and 'will seize'→'would seize'. Option A is the cleverest distractor — it swaps 'unless' for 'until', changing a conditional clause into a temporal one and completely altering the meaning. Option C omits backshift in the subordinate clause, retaining 'will repay'. Option D uses ungrammatical 'said me' and also fails to backshift 'will seize'.
